transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Redwood Infra), Dr. Lisa Park (CTO OpenHealthCare), Marco Ruiz (ML Platform Lead), Sofia Chen (Data Engineering), Daniel Mbatha (Security)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive into long-context performance for 128k+ prompts. Focus on runtime approaches: chunking/streaming, KV cache management, batching vs latency, quantization strategies, and private deployment networking. Action items and next steps captured at end.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we've got about 75 minutes on the agenda, main goal is to walk through architecture options for 128k context use cases, show expected perf, and agree on a benchmark plan.
[00:18] Dr. Lisa Park: thanks Alex, yeah we're excited — our main two concerns are latency for interactive workflows and the storage/cost of keeping patient histories in context, plus security for on-prem.
[00:30] Marco: hi all, we run a mix of live triage flows and batch summarization, the 128k use case is mostly for cross-visit synthesis and long longitudinal notes. We care a lot about deterministic behavior too.
[00:45] Priya: perfect, i'll jump into the runtime considerations then, but quick question on success criteria: do you want p50 interactive under 300ms or is throughput more important for you?
[00:55] Sofia: for triage interactive p99 under 1s would be ideal, but we can accept higher for non-interactive workflows. Cost per 1k tokens is also a hard req for procurement.
[01:10] Alex: noted. ok priya over to you.
[01:15] Priya: cool, so for 128k contexts we usually combine chunking + KV cache. The high level — we stream in the most recent window to the attention layer and materialize older context as key/value cache entries. That avoids re-attending over the full 128k each request.
[01:35] Priya: caveats — KV cache sizing matters: if the workload has many distinct threads per user, the KV cache can grow quickly. We recommend per-customer capped cache with LRU + weighted eviction to keep working set small.
[01:52] Dr. Lisa Park: when you say chunking, is that semantic chunking or fixed-size? we've got a lot of structured fields and section headers in notes.
[02:03] Priya: good call, we typically do hybrid. Fixed-size chunks for low-cost indexing but a semantic layer on top — e.g., split on sections/encounters, keep chunk boundaries aligned with clinical notes. That helps reconstruction and reduces cross-chunk attention shattering.
[02:25] Marco: how does that affect hallucination risk when we stitch chunks back together?
[02:32] Priya: stitching can introduce missing cross-chunk dependencies — to mitigate we include summary vectors (dense embeddings) for each chunk and optionally run a short cross-attention pass over chunk summaries. It's cheaper than attending to full tokens.
[02:48] Ethan: to add, our continuous batching pipeline can form batches across similar sequence-length requests to improve GPU utilization while keeping tail latency reasonable — batching window default is 20ms but we can tune up to 50-100ms depending on SLAs.
[03:05] Sofia: 20ms sounds small; will that hit our p99?
[03:10] Ethan: the impact on p99 depends on traffic shape. We do adaptive batching: during low QPS it prioritizes latency (small windows), during sustained throughput it increases window to boost throughput. There's always tradeoffs.
[03:25] Priya: also quantization: INT8/4-bit quantization reduces memory footprint and improves throughput, but there is a small accuracy delta on certain instructions. We have verified configs for a number of open models where accuracy loss is negligible for summarization, but for clinical extraction you might want FP16 or mixed quant.
[03:48] Dr. Lisa Park: what's the perf delta roughly for 128k scenarios?
[03:53] Priya: ballpark — INT8 can give 1.8x-2.5x throughput improvement and reduce KV cache memory by ~45%, but you should run evals; we can share the quant profiles.
[04:10] Marco: are there models that break with quantization? we've seen entity extraction accuracy drop in our internal tests.
[04:18] Priya: yes, low-rank adapter-heavy finetunes and some token-level classifiers can be sensitive. Our recommendation: run an AB test on a held-out eval set. We'll provide the recommended quantization matrix per model.
[04:31] Alex: let's talk attention optimizations — flash-attn, sparse attention variants, and kernel selection. Priya, Ethan?
[04:40] Ethan: flash-attn style kernels drastically reduce memory and time for causal attention when sequence lengths are large. For 128k we combine flash-attn with chunked local attention windows and occasional global tokens to maintain cross-chunk context.
[04:57] Priya: we also implement attention caching and compressed KV encodings. For example we can compress older KV slots with a lightweight quantized representation and decompress on demand. That trades CPU for memory.
[05:12] Marco: is decompression on demand noticeable in latency?
[05:16] Ethan: depends on frequency; if you decompress on every request it's costly. Instead we keep a hot set of recently used chunks uncompressed and lazily decompress as access patterns dictate.
[05:28] [05:28] Sofia: can you give an example of config for a triage flow? like how many chunks, cache size?
[05:33] Priya: typical triage: recent 8-12 chunks hot in memory (~8-32k tokens), KV cache cap per user ~200k tokens depending on budget. Chunking size we recommend 1k-4k tokens per chunk for clinical notes.
[05:50] Alex: ok we'll capture those numbers in the benchmark config.
[05:56] Dr. Lisa Park: let's move to VPC/on-prem — our security team is concerned about KMS integration and audit logs.
[06:05] Daniel: yes we need to ensure customer-managed keys, and full audit trails for both model inputs and system events. Also ping time to any on-prem HSM could be high and impact latency.
[06:18] Alex: we support customer-managed KMS for private deployments, and we can integrate with on-prem HSMs in our Private offering. That does mean the call to KMS introduces an extra round-trip for key unwrap — we usually cache decrypted keys in secure enclave for the duration of a session to avoid per-request KMS calls.
[06:36] Priya: for audit logs we can stream to your SIEM or S3 bucket; we expose token-level metadata but can redact PII on ingestion if required.
[06:47] Marco: network wise, what are latencies if we run Redwood Private in our VPC versus dedicated hosted?
[06:54] Ethan: with VPC peering in same region we typically see sub-5ms intra-region latency to the endpoint; on-prem over VPN or transit can be 10-50ms depending on circuits. The bigger cost is cold cache misses that require preloading large KV sets.
[07:12] Sofia: preloading — can we warm caches ahead of time?
[07:15] Priya: yes, we provide pre-warm jobs that materialize KV entries for a cohort of users before traffic hits. This can be scheduled nightly or triggered by events.
[07:25] [07:25] Marco: about benchmarks — what artifacts do you need from our side?
[07:28] Alex: we'll need representative prompt sets, sample documents, desired SLAs, and cost targets. Also expected concurrency and traffic patterns. Marco will share 2 prompt sets and S3 link.
[07:40] Marco: noted, will share by Friday.
[07:45] Priya: we'll produce a benchmark plan: 1) synthetic 128k worst-case run, 2) customer-sampled workload, 3) accuracy/regression tests vs base model. We'll give expected metrics: p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cost per 1M tokens.
[08:05] Dr. Lisa Park: about chunking heuristics — can you control chunk size adaptively? some of our notes are very short, others are huge.
[08:15] Priya: yes adaptive chunking can be rule-based: min/max chunk size, prefer semantic boundaries, merge short documents into a chunk, split huge ones, and adjust on-the-fly based on token distribution. We can expose tuning knobs in Redwood Optimize.
[08:32] Sofia: you mentioned embedding summaries earlier — do you store embeddings separately and do dot-product retrieval?
[08:38] Priya: yes, embeddings for chunk summaries and a FAISS-style index for retrieval. We use dense retrieval to find relevant chunks and then bring those into the hot window. This reduces attention scope.
[08:55] Marco: retrieval latency then becomes a factor; do you do async prefetch?
[09:00] Ethan: we have an async prefetch pipeline — fetch likely chunks based on initial query embeddings, start decompressing KV, and if missing do a fall-back to slower retrieval. It's probabilistic but effective.
[09:14] [09:14] Alex: let's walk through an example flow end-to-end for a triage query.
[09:18] Priya: user query -> embed -> retrieve top-8 chunk summaries -> prefetch hot chunks -> build request with recent tokens + hot chunk KV pointers -> runtime executes with flash-attn kernels -> partial streaming of output. If cross-chunk signals are required we do a summary-attention pass on chunk summaries.
[09:43] Marco: what's the cost/latency of the summary-attention pass?
[09:48] Priya: it's tiny relative to full attention — usually an extra 10-30ms depending on model and summary length.
[09:56] Sofia: i'd like to see numbers for our data.
[09:59] Alex: we'll run the POC benchmarks and produce a table for p50/p95/p99 and cost.
[10:05] Dr. Lisa Park: how about model fallbacks or graceful degradation? if the Dedicated pool is saturated, can we auto-fallback to a smaller model?
[10:14] Ethan: yes, smart routing can fallback to lighter quantized variants or smaller models, we can route based on latency SLOs and cost policies. We keep versions pinned at route-level so it's predictable.
[10:27] Marco: for private deployments, is fallback across environments supported? e.g., if private is down can we use hosted?
[10:35] Alex: in Private we can configure cross-environment fallback but that requires policy approval for data residency; you can fall back to a sanitized model that doesn't persist PII, or use tokenization/redaction before leaving VPC.
[10:49] Daniel: that raises compliance questions, we may not allow egress. We'll need a full design doc.
[10:56] Alex: understood — action to send security docs and network diagram.
[11:01] [11:01] Priya: back to quantization: one operational trick — we shard KV cache across GPUs using 2D partitioning, with compressed storage on NVMe for cold pages. That lets us keep hot pages in GPU memory and spill cold ones to NVMe, decompressing into host RAM when needed.
[11:23] Marco: that sounds I/O heavy. how do you keep tail latency in check?
[11:27] Ethan: we use async IO + prefetch heuristics, and we preemptively warm cold pages based on predicted access patterns. Worst-case tail can spike but we throttle and return degraded results with a warning instead of full failure.
[11:42] Sofia: can we restrict per-user memory so a heavy user doesn't cause eviction for others?
[11:47] Priya: yes multi-tenant caps and QoS layers — per-user caps, per-route priorities, and throttling. For Dedicated you can also reserve a guaranteed portion of KV RAM per customer.
[12:01] Marco: curious about sequence length distribution in your tests — do you test uniform 128k or more realistic skewed workloads?
[12:08] Priya: both. Synthetic uniform stresses GPU memory and attention kernels; realistic skewed workloads show different batching characteristics and cache hit rates. We run both types during benchmarks.
[12:20] Alex: can you run a synthetic 128k worst-case and a customer-sampled workload side-by-side?
[12:25] Priya: yes we'll do both and report.
[12:29] [12:29] Dr. Lisa Park: if we want deterministic outputs for audits, is there a recommended config?
[12:35] Priya: set seeds, pin model versions, disable dynamic sampling in generation, and avoid quantization configs that introduce non-determinism. Note some kernel optimizations (e.g., fused ops) can change numerics slightly; we'll document exactly what changes were made.
[12:53] Marco: what about eval infrastructure—how do you compare accuracy across quantization levels?
[12:58] Priya: we run token-level metrics and downstream task metrics (e.g., entity F1, summary ROUGE), and we surface regression alerts for any metric delta beyond a threshold. We'll run your clinical extraction tests.
[13:14] Sofia: network encryption — do you support mutual TLS + client certs for private?
[13:18] Ethan: yes mTLS, SAML SSO, and optional client certs. We also support VPC peering and private link equivalents.
[13:29] Dr. Lisa Park: ok good. procurement will want pricing on Dedicated vs Private.
[13:34] Alex: we'll include pricing bands in the follow-up along with expected unit economics from the benchmark.
[13:40] [13:40] Marco: edge case — what if a single document is 1M tokens? do you stream or chunk?
[13:47] Priya: we chunk and stream — we never attempt to process 1M tokens in a single attention graph. We process sequential chunks and maintain a sliding KV context. That also enables partial outputs as we go.
[13:58] Sofia: how do you handle tokenization boundary issues across chunk splits?
[14:03] Priya: we overlap chunk boundaries by a small margin (e.g., 32-64 tokens) and use anchor tokens to avoid splitting entities. Semantic chunkers also try to respect sentence boundaries.
[14:18] Marco: for clinical records we need redaction rules before indexing — can Redwood apply PII redaction pre-ingest?
[14:25] Alex: yes we have ingestion pipelines that can apply redaction, token-level masking, or hashing prior to storage. We can discuss the rules offline with your security team.
[14:37] Daniel: also need to know data retention for cached KV — how long do you keep hot pages?
[14:42] Priya: retention is configurable per customer; default is 24h for hot cache, with cold persisted compressed for up to configurable period (30-90 days) depending on compliance. We also support immediate purge on request.
[14:57] [14:57] Alex: ok let's pivot to the concrete benchmark setup — priya can you outline the test plan?
[15:02] Priya: test plan: 1) synthetic worst-case 128k throughput test (single-session long sequence) across 3 GPU configs; 2) sampled customer workload with concurrency ramp to expected QPS; 3) accuracy/quant test across FP16, INT8, and mixed; 4) cold-start and prewarm runs to measure warmup time. We'll produce CSVs with p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU mem, NVMe IO, and cost estimates.
[15:29] Marco: which GPU configs? A100, H100, and one cost-optimized like L4?
[15:35] Ethan: we'll run H100 + sGPU optimized kernels (best perf), A100, and a cost-optimized instance (e.g., L4) to show tradeoffs. H100 gives best throughput on large context with flash-attn.
[15:48] Sofia: expected time to run?
[15:50] Priya: synthetic runs can finish in a day, customer-sampled maybe 2-3 days to get stable numbers. We'll prioritize the synthetic and one customer sample first.
[16:01] Alex: action recap: Alex to run initial synthetic benchmark on Redwood Dedicated with sample data; Priya to share quant profiles and test matrix; Ethan to provide recommended batching/KV config; customer to share prompt sets and S3 link by 2026-06-18.
[16:20] [16:20] Dr. Lisa Park: open question about fallback policy in Private if we cannot allow any egress — how do we handle capacity spikes?
[16:28] Priya: we can provision burst capacity inside your VPC (reserved spare GPUs) or enable internal degraded mode where we serve shorter contexts to keep latency but drop older context. It's a policy decision.
[16:44] Marco: does Redwood have any recommended heuristics for dropping older context (time-based vs relevance-based)?
[16:50] Priya: relevance-based is best: keep recent and high-similarity chunks; older low-similarity ones can be purged. Time-based TTL is simpler but less precise.
[17:04] Sofia: any gotchas with model sharding across GPUs for KV?
[17:09] Ethan: cross-GPU all-reduce for attention keys can be expensive; we prefer 2D sharding where feasible to reduce cross-node comms. Also avoid small micro-batches that amplify comm overhead.
[17:23] Alex: alright we're nearing the end — let's surface outstanding questions and owners.
[17:29] Daniel: security DOC and network diagram (Alex).
[17:32] Marco: we'll need a compliance checklist for Private deployment (SOC2 controls mapping).
[17:36] Alex: noted. Priya: i'll add compliance checklist and quant matrix to the deliverables.
[17:44] [17:44] Sofia: one practical ask — can you include sample Redwood config file showing KV cache caps, chunk size, and batching settings?
[17:50] Priya: yes we'll include a sample config and recommended starting values.
[17:55] Alex: last thing — cost modeling: we'll include per-token cost estimates for each GPU profile and expected monthly spend for projected QPS.
[18:05] Dr. Lisa Park: great. thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[18:12] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and security pack.
[18:20] Priya: thanks everyone, bye.

Recap & Next steps:
- Redwood to run synthetic 128k benchmark on Dedicated + submit results (Alex)
- Priya to share quant profiles, sample Redwood config, and test matrix (Priya)
- Ethan to provide batching/KV config recommendations and expected warmup times (Ethan)
- OpenHealthCare to share prompt sets + S3 read-only access (Marco)
- Redwood to send SOC2/security pack and network diagram (Alex)

References mentioned: QUIC prefetch, flash-attn, FAISS, KV cache spill to NVMe, customer will receive a benchmark CSV and config.

End of transcript.
